title: Recursion
overview: Recursion is when a routine calls itself to solve a smaller version of a problem. A valid recursive solution needs a stopping/base case and guaranteed progress toward it. You must trace calls, explain the call stack and unwinding, and evaluate recursion against iterative alternatives.
syllabusPoints: Explain the essential features of recursion.
Explain when recursion is an appropriate solution technique.
Explain call-stack storage and unwinding of recursive calls.

definitions.definition: A condition that returns a result without making another recursive call.
The part that calls the same routine on a smaller/closer-to-base problem.
The LIFO stack storing active routine calls, parameters, local data and return points.
Returning from nested recursive calls in reverse order after the base case is reached.

sections.title: Designing a recursive routine
content: Every possible recursive path must eventually reach a base case. The recursive case should reduce the problem—such as n becoming n-1 or a tree call moving to a child. Otherwise recursion continues until stack space is exhausted.

examples.label: Cambridge-style pseudocode
examples.content:
FUNCTION Factorial(n)
  IF n=0 THEN
    RETURN 1
  ELSE
    RETURN n*Factorial(n-1)
  ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION

sections.title: Tracing calls
content: Separate the downward call phase from the upward return phase. Each call waits while the next is evaluated; once the base result appears, returns are resolved in reverse order.

sections.title: Call stack
content: Each active invocation needs a stack frame containing parameters/local variables and a return address. Because the stack is LIFO, the latest call finishes first during unwinding.

sections.title: When recursion is useful
content: It is natural for recursively defined structures/problems such as trees, divide-and-conquer algorithms or nested directory structures. For simple repetition, iteration can use less memory because it avoids many active stack frames.

examTips: If a recursive routine never stops, check base case AND whether the argument actually approaches it.
Trace calls down and returns up explicitly.
When evaluating recursion, mention readability/natural structure as well as memory/stack overhead.
commonMistakes: Having a base case but continuing to recurse inside it.
Assuming returns occur in creation order rather than LIFO.
Claiming recursion is always faster than iteration.
